idea: The great flourished 'B' initial from the Mainz Psalter, redrawn in one ink, captioned 'The first book to print its own birthday: 14 August 1457.' Fust and Schoeffer's Psalter was the first printed book with a dated colophon naming its printers, so this is a gorgeous letter that is also a birth certificate for publishing.

Andrea Alciato's 'In silentium' woodcut of a scholar in his study with a finger to his lips, with his couplet in English: 'When he's silent, a fool is no different from the wise.' It comes from the 1531 Emblemata, the first emblem book, and makes a dry case for saying less.

Comenius's woodcut lamb from the alphabet page of Orbis Pictus, with the 1659 English text: 'The Lamb blaiteth. bé é é. B b.' The first picture book made for children taught each letter as an animal noise (the crow 'crieth á á' for A), which is charming and also a real teaching method.

One engraved capital from the Romain du Roi, Louis XIV's royal alphabet of the 1690s, laid on its fine construction grid, captioned 'A king ordered a typeface. A committee drew it on 2,304 squares.' The Académie des sciences committee really did plot letters on a grid of 64 squares each split into 36, and it's a beautiful ancestor of every digital font.

George Herbert's 'Easter Wings' as it was printed in The Temple in 1633: turned sideways across the page so the lines form two pairs of wings, captioned 'Printed sideways so the poem could fly.' It's an early shaped poem where the layout is part of the meaning.

The wobbly plot diagrams Laurence Sterne drew in Tristram Shandy (Vol. VI, ch. 40) to show how his story wandered through earlier volumes, then his single ruled line, with his words: 'I may arrive hereafter at the excellency of going on even thus.' A 1760s novelist drawing infographics of his own digressions, for anyone whose life plan looks like a scribble.

A page of Irish minuscule from the 9th-century Reichenau Primer with a small white cat drawn pouncing on one letter, captioned 'Pangur Bán. Hunting mice is his delight; hunting words is mine.' The Old Irish poem by a monk about his cat, written in that manuscript, is a perfect picture of quiet work done side by side.

Arcimboldo's 'The Librarian' (c. 1566), the portrait of a man built entirely from books, with open pages for hair and bookmarks for fingers, captioned 'Made of what he read.' A witty Renaissance painting that turns 'you are what you read' into a face.

One woodcut city view from the 1493 Nuremberg Chronicle printed four times in a row and labelled DAMASCUS, FERRARA, MILAN, MANTUA. The book really did reuse the same block for all four cities, getting 1,809 pictures out of 645 woodblocks, which makes it the first stock image and a sly joke about mass media.

Cochin's frontispiece to Diderot's Encyclopédie, with Truth unveiled by Reason and Philosophy in a temple of light, captioned 'Banned in 1759. Finished anyway.' The Encyclopédie lost its royal privilege and was put on the papal Index in 1759, and the editors kept going, so it's about knowledge that won't be stopped.

A line of Baskerville roman from his specimen with the small text: 'A critic said Baskerville's type would blind readers. Franklin showed him a Caslon specimen with the name torn off. He said it hurt his eyes.' Benjamin Franklin told the story in a 1760 letter to Baskerville, and it's a typography joke about snobbery that type people will love.

The frontispiece of the Diamond Sutra from Dunhuang, the Buddha preaching under a canopy, with its colophon translated: 'Made for universal free distribution. 11 May 868.' It's the oldest dated printed book known, and its first line about sharing for free is a point of view on open access almost 1,200 years old.

A page of flourished calligraphy from Mira calligraphiae monumenta, Georg Bocskay's 1561–62 model book, with one of Joris Hoefnagel's beetles sitting on the letters, captioned 'The scribe showed off. Thirty years later a painter added a bug.' Hoefnagel did illuminate the book in the 1590s, and it's a lovely duel between writing and drawing.

Christophe Plantin's printer's mark, a hand from the clouds holding a pair of compasses, with the motto 'LABORE ET CONSTANTIA' and the key: 'The fixed leg is constancy. The moving leg is work.' It's the device of the Golden Compasses press in Antwerp, and a 16th-century motto for anyone working on something long.

A woven border and initial from the 1896 Kelmscott Chaucer, framing William Morris's line 'Have nothing in your houses that you do not know to be useful, or believe to be beautiful.' Morris said it in 1880, then started his own press at 57 to make books by that rule, so the shirt follows its own advice.

An engraving of a 17th-century hornbook (a wooden paddle holding the alphabet and the Lord's Prayer under a thin sheet of clear horn), captioned 'Handheld. Shatterproof screen. One app.' Generations of children learned to read on them, and the joke points out that the reading tablet is not a new idea.

Mallarmé's 'Un coup de dés' spread, its words scattered across the page in different sizes, with only the translation of its spine phrase: 'A throw of the dice will never abolish chance.' The 1897 poem made white space part of the text, and its line about chance sits naturally beside a Lorenz attractor.

The engraved title page of the Index Librorum Prohibitorum, the Church's list of banned books, captioned '1559–1966. The longest-running reading list in history.' Galileo, Descartes and Kant were all on it, so the shirt turns a censor's list into a recommendation.

The title page of Robert Cawdrey's 1604 'A Table Alphabeticall', the first monolingual English dictionary, with its real subtitle picked out: 'for the benefit & helpe of Ladies, Gentlewomen, or any other unskilfull persons.' A dictionary of about 2,500 hard words with a cheeky 400-year-old put-down built in.

A plate from William Blake's Jerusalem with its line in his own hand-etched lettering: 'I must Create a System, or be enslav'd by another Mans.' Blake invented relief etching so he could print his words and pictures on the same copper plate himself, so the line fits the method behind it: an independent-maker shirt.
